text:
I received an advanced copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for an honest review. 
 I only wish I had better things to say. If you like your mysteries to be convoluted and the police work to be shoddy and the plot to be just about implausible, you'll like this book. 
 Deadly Bonds was my introduction to the "Detective Jackson" series--and it appears to be the ninth or tenth book in the series. This book receives 2 stars from me -- 1 star being a benefit of the doubt round-up, as this is part of a series, and maybe if I had read the previous ones, I could have overlooked some of this book's flaws. But as a stand alone, it didn't work for me. I couldn't connect with the main characters and didn't feel compelled by the plot. It's never a good sign for me when I realize I don't care who killed the victims or how exactly they died--which shows I didn't care for the minor characters, either. 
 Some examples of why this book just didn't work for me: 
 .At the beginning of this book, the reader is introduced to characters they must have known from previous books, because the author doesn't bother to really introduce them here. Kera, Detective Jackson's girlfriend, is mentioned at the beginning of the book when she's in the hospital because her grandson's baby-mommy and baby-mommy's football playing boyfriend are in the hospital, and the baby-mommy is on life support. (A red herring--they have nothing to do with anything and merely serve as an example of the overly complex nature of the relationships in this book.). But Detective Jackson is busy with a case, so he can't visit Kera or deal with her situation at the moment. It seems like literally 100 pages pass between mentions of this woman, so much so that when her name came up, I thought, "Who's Kera?" Yet he loves her, and she's a wonderful woman. The author hasn't bothered to show me that, but it is mentioned repeatedly... so it must be true. (Sigh.) 
 Then there are the two crimes, which up until about 60% seem unconnected. At the point they finally do connect, I had already checked out of the investigation, but was simply determined to finish this book. Crime one: A young woman is found strangled in a foreclosed house, and crime two: a football player for UO is found dead in his bathroom of a heart attack. The investigation into these deaths take a bunch of crazy turns, most of which are red herrings. Maybe this is the way police work actually goes, but that doesn't make me trust the intelligence of these detectives. The list of random suspects includes a teenage boy (suspected because the police find a knife which clearly wasn't used in the crime...), an older couple from Utah traveling around in their RV (which must be a very fast-moving RV indeed, for them to be suspected of being present at the crime scenes, despite the fact that no witnesses saw an RV in the area), a drug dealer named Marcos (who is hauled off to the PD and apparently forgotten in a holding cell, because he's never mentioned again), the dead football player's ex-girlfriend (who is just mean, apparently), and the dead football player's pregnant girlfriend (because ... oh, it doesn't matter). And then out of the blue, there's crime three: the attempted kidnapping of dead-woman-in-foreclosed-home's son, which spawns crime four: actual kidnapping of Detective Jackson's runaway teenage daughter. There's an explanation given for the kidnapper's involvement with the case, although in the end, medical evidence proves the explanation to be false. (Read: Opening for next book in series.) 
 But my biggest issue had to be with the handling of the dead woman's three-year-old son. I'm no expert on police procedural or on child protective services or child custody, admittedly, so I'm just going off common sense here. Detective Jackson lost all credibility with me when he decided he could care for the three-year-old boy, and removed him from the proper care channels. No matter that his personal life is a mess (nice girlfriend in hospital hoping grandson's baby-mamma survives), or that he's in the middle of an investigation and has to cart the boy with him all over town, popping earphones on the kid's head so he doesn't hear anything traumatic about his mother's death. Since he clearly needs help dealing with the boy when he's in the middle of the case and has to fly from Oregon to Utah, who better to call than his estranged runaway teenage daughter with a drinking problem, who seems to care only about meeting up with her latest boyfriend and checking her cell phone? If someone--cough, member of the court, cough--were truly looking out for three-year-old-kid's best interest, s/he would have pointed out that Detective Jackson had no right to custody, had no right to leave the child in the care of his less than reliable daughter, should not have toted the kid around town to various crime scenes, and finally--should not have used the kid in a hostage exchange, clearly endangering said kid's life. But without this horrific lapse of common sense, there wouldn't have been much of a story--which makes the kid feel like nothing more than a thirty-pound plot device. .. 
 I will say I kind of liked Evans, though.

The year is 1786. John Holdsworth is the widow of a woman who believed in ghosts, at least following the death of their son. John could not share her beliefs. In fact, he went out of his way to disprove them, writing a book, The Anatomy of Ghosts. It is this book that catches the attention of a wealthy woman whose son needs help after a (ghost related) breakdown. Down on his luck, John is persuaded to offer this help and heads to Cambridge where the son, Frank, is a student at Jerusalem College. What he finds there is the story of a dead woman that isn't quite what it seems. 
 The Anatomy of Ghosts is a murder mystery more than it is a ghost story and an enjoyable one at that. It is well written and draws a picture of a time when academia was not as highly valued as it is now and when money and wealth let you get away with a lot. I feel I should have liked reading it more, but this might be because of how much I was expecting from the author of The American Boy. All in all, however, a good read and a book I would recommend to others.

text:
I have to say I don't think I was the right audience for this book. 
 I enjoy books that are set in other places and which feature travelers as main characters because I want the setting to also function like a character. While that was true for Nightmare in Morocco, I found that I was not receptive to a book in which the exotic setting is itself a villain. 
 Nightmare in Morocco is about a young American travel guide who lives in Spain. Her boss pleads with her to guide a tour to Morocco just once, but she is haunted by a bad experience traveling in that country as a child. She agrees to do the tour, even though a family tragedy occurs and she is left as the guardian for her wild step-niece. The main character, Noa, is understandably stressed by several factors--her job and her recent family problems, for example. However, she spends so much of the book dwelling on her childhood trauma in Morocco (she got lost in a bazaar) that it made me question how the character could believably have chosen to be a tour guide as a profession. For someone who had supposedly lived and traveled abroad almost since birth, according to the backstory, it was hard for me to accept that Noa would be so prejudiced and socially sheltered. 
 Because, though there are also human baddies, Morocco itself is a sinister presence in the book. And, I don't think I was the right reader for that kind of story. 
 Nightmare in Morocco is a short read and contains both a mystery and a romance. The romance was more fun than the mystery for me, though I enjoyed following the threads of the plot in both. Several of the characters are also enjoyable, and some of the scenes that feature a more lighthearted atmosphere--such as the camel ride--are fun to visualize. 
 I wouldn't recommend this book as travel inspiration for Morocco (a country which I have, in fact, visited), but if you are looking for a shorter read in a 1980s-style romance, take a look. 
 I received a copy of Nightmare in Morocco in exchange for a review.

text: I really wanted to enjoy this book (I received a free First reads copy from Goodreads) but I just couldn't. No part of this book stood up to scrutiny, so every time I was forced to suspend my disbelief by more logical inconsistencies, I'm afraid I was not inclined to do so. My main issues with the book were the characters, who were rather unlikeable, as much as they had personalities, as many of them came and went too quickly for me to have any concern for their fate. Two characters in particular were supposed to be professionals, with specific expertise, but were often shocked at perfectly predictable turns of events. The technological elements of the story were trying to be central, but ultimately did not seem to be fully understood by the author, and the slightly clumsy use made this stand out. As a reader (and viewer) of many a thriller, I waited for something new, something compelling, but I was at a loss. The one part that mostly worked was the structure of short chapters, timed and location marked, giving some sense of freneticism, but on several occasions, the crucial timings did not add up. One final minor point- it contained the term 'hanged' in place of 'hung' on more than one occasion, which just looked poor.

I usually stay away from legal/crime dramas but a friend recommened this book to me and I'm glad she did. What an exciting read! Despite it's length, I thought the story moved quickly and the strategically placed foreshadowing propelled me right to the end. 
 I don't want to give away much on the plot so simply the book is about a DA lawyer named Andy Barber whose son Jacob is charged with the murder of one of his classmates in the town of Newton MA. Andy Barber is telling us this story from a grand jury testimony that is conducted after the trial which is why there is some foreshadowing. And so begins the rocky road to the trial for the Barber family who basically become isolated by the town. 
 I felt that Landay really gave us the opportunity to understand the Barber family which includes Andy's wife Laurie. You could feel the mental toll the arrest has on the family and the need for a verdict. The twist ending had me surprised despite what might have been hints to it throughout the story. 
 Even if you're not a crime buff, I think most would like this story. The legal aspects are not extremely technical but clearly the author knows his stuff and to me finds success in providing an exciting murder mystery.

Esta novela no se lee, en esta novela se vive.

Al autor le cabe todo en la novela: asesinos en serie, las carceles, los bares, la mafia china, la prostitucion, el acoso escolar, la infidelidad, el alcoholismo, la violencia domestica, los gitanos, los canis con perros, los gorilas de los garitos...todo ello adobado con las noticias mas destacadas de la epoca y otra infinidad de datos dispares e insolitos en forma de rafaga. Y Carabanchel, sobre todo Carabanchel, omnipresente como epitome de todos los barrios de extrarradio de las grandes ciudades. 
 La estructura es original, envolvente y rompedora, como un caleidoscopio de historias: simultaneas, yuxtapuestas, todas ellas interesantes y singulares pero que giran alrededor de tres o cuatro personajes principales: Greta Santamaria y Marcelo Saravia, Susana Coelho y el arabe, y, sobre todo Max Luminaria, el carismatico asesino en serie de la moneda, un Jack el destripador contemporaneo del que conoceremos todos sus pensamientos, pulsiones, deseos y hasta el ultimo recoveco de su mente . Por el estilo me recuerda a Mazurca para dos muertos de Camilo Jose Cela. Es una novela muy negra y mas adictiva que el pegamento en bolsa. Esta plagada de actos criminales y sexo sucio y duro, o sea bien hecho como diria Woody Allen. 
 Hacedme caso, haced un alto en vuestra lista de lecturas y arrojaos de cabeza a "Te quiero porque me das de comer" me lo vais a agradecer. Si el autor hubiera sido americano ya seria conocido mundialmente y le habrian llovido los premios y las adaptaciones al cine o a la television de sus obras, pero claro es lo que tiene ser de Carabanchel que no tienes tanto eco.

text:
Cleverly written, this book is full of surprises. It will lead you down the rabbit hole and feels like you'll never meet the ground. 
 Maggie Rose is a lawyer and true crime writer who's known for overturning convictions of murderers to set them free. At first glance you wouldn't guess that she's a lawyer. Her bright blue hair, reclusive tendencies and refusal to do court or press appearances put her more on the quirky side than a professional lawyer. But what is it about her that allows her to find loopholes to put enough doubts in crime investigations to set convicts free? 
 Hamish Wolfe has been in jail for the last two years for the murder of four women. He claims he's innocent. So does the fan group lead by his mother. His charm and good looks has amassed a following who's devoted to setting him free. They're focused on bringing Maggie in to do the same. 
 The author uses letters, newspaper clips, and other articles to give the many perspectives on these characters and what occurred to put Wolfe behind bars. There are lots of questions that arise as you're reading so they keep you wondering and guessing. I started to work things out in my head but even then the events unfolding still surprised me. 
 Looking forward to reading more from this author.

text:
What'd I think? I think this was a superb read! I say this every time I give a book five stars but I really so rarely do. There's something about a book that makes me block out everything in space and time, forego food and other habits because I just can't put it down. I NEED to know what happens. 
 The Silent Sister is vividly written, moderately paced. Parts of this story are told through Lisa's POV, which was enlightening. Watching the details bob to the surface and the two POV's dovetail to reveal the huge, devastating mystery was sheer entertainment. 
 Of all of the characters, I think I felt the most sympathy for Riley's brother, Danny. Caught between the horrors of war and the tearing apart of his family, his anger and anxiety are palpable, his discomfort jumping off of the page. His deep love for his sister redeems his cold and calculating demeanor and his final act of love toward her was so benevolent, it brought tears to my eyes. 
 The Silent Sister was an excellent, perfect read. I really enjoyed it.

text:
4 stars 
 My first Lisa Clark O'Neill book and it certainly won't be the last. I like her writing style, quick and easy to read without overthinking things much. The dialogue between the H/h is also clever and fun with some tease and sarcasm. The main and secondary characters are all likable. 
 I had expected this to read more like a romantic suspense novel but I thought it leaned towards contemporary romance with a dash of mystery thrown in. For some reason, I thought this was a procedural book. While there was some elements of "detective" work, the focus was more on the relationships around these characters. The build up between Jordan and Ava's relationship was slow and sweet. Ava was a bit hesitant at Jordan's advances but he knows how to wear her down. I mean honestly, how do you turn away from a man who rescues and adopts a stray dog? :) 
 There wasn't much to go on to guess "whodunit" as you barely get a glimpse from the killer's POV but the author tied up the loose ends nicely at the end. 
 I'll be back to visit this series again soon.

text:
Robert Hunter in seinem Buro angerufen. Am anderen Ende der Leitung: Ein Mann, der mit dem Detective von Mord 1 ein Spiel spielen will. Uber eine Website, die nur Hunter und sein Partner Garcia einsehen konnen, sehen sie einen Mann in einem Glascontainer. Hunter muss entscheiden, wie der Mann sterben soll: verbrennen oder ertrinken. 
 Und es bleibt nicht bei diesem einen Spiel. Uber die Todesart des nachsten Opfers soll die Internetgemeinde live abstimmen, wahrend Hunter und Garcia nichts tun konnen ausser zusehen. Eine Jagd gegen die Zeit beginnt, denn der Tater hat bereits das nachste Opfer im Visier. 
 Wow. Was fur eine Story. Und wie makabar und wahnsinnig. Ich denke jedes Mal, dass Carter sich mit dem Wahnsinn seiner Morder nicht mehr steigern kann, und dann prasentiert er mir im nachsten Buch ein Exemplar von Serienmorder, das die Vorangegangenen beinahe in den Schatten stellt. Bei diesem Morder kommt eine spezielle Art der Grausamkeit hinzu, er qualt nicht nur die Opfer, er lasst auch Hunter und Garcia leiden indem er sie tatenlos zusehen lasst, und macht die Internetgemeinde ebenfalls zu kollektiven Mitschuldigen an der Tat. Man hat auch keine Chance, den Morder zu erraten, denn die Hintergrundstory dazu bleibt selbst fur die beiden Detectives sehr lange im Dunkeln. Gemeinerweise ist es beim Totschlager ahnlich wie beim Totenkunstler: Man verabscheut die Taten, aber bis zu einem gewissen Grat kann man erkennen und nachvollziehen, warum der Tater so gehandelt hat. Der Fall wirft Fragen auf, wie weit das Internet gehen kann, ob und welche moralischen Grundsatze dort gelten, wie man mit Grausamkeit im Netz umgeht, usw. Der Thriller hangt mir nach knapp einer Woche immer noch nach, und uber manche Aspekte werde ich noch einige Zeit grubeln, weil sie mir auch in meinem Leben immer wieder begegnen. 
 Vom Klischee her sollen Thriller nur unterhalten, das Genre ist eher weniger dafur bekannt, zum Nachdenken anzuregen. Doch genau das ist bei diesem Fall von Hunter und Garcia passiert. Hut ab. Der Totschlager ist der bisher mit Abstand beste Chris Carter!

text:
Lacey Flint is asked to work undercover as a student at Cambridge University and find out why so many students are committing suicide...and not just in your "run of the mill" way. They are setting fire to themselves, decapitating themselves, hanging themselves from trees. The theory is that there is someone egging people on, most likely some type of online group who are praying on the vulnerable. Lacey's job is to pretend to be vulnerable and see what happens. It isn't to investigate. She can't help herself though and curiosity drives her to dig deeper and deeper until she finds she might be the next victim. 
 I like S J Bolton and have read her other books - other than Lacey Flint #1 - and really enjoyed them. This one left me a little cold I'm afraid. It just didn't seem completely thought out. The ending felt tacked on to provide a last bit of jeopardy for Lacey, who was actually quite annoying. She is supposed to be a detective and yet doesn't see what is happening right in front of her and makes what seem like really silly mistakes. Not much more can be said for the other characters either. Overall, disappointed.

text: My friends tease me that my interests in film and literature focus on the tragic, horrific, and unfortunate. The book Columbine does not disappoint on this front. I liked three aspects of this book in particular. First, a blow by blow description of what happened that day is provided. Second the author dispels many rumors and falsehoods that were propagated by the press. For example, did you know that the killers were not outcasts and victims of bullying as so often reported? Third, the author pieces together disparate pieces of information in an attempt to explain why these teenage boys killed. Sadly, the Colobine tragedy did not stop Virginia Tech or Sandy Hook from happening but I understand the matter better and that is a start.

text:
No One Heard Her Scream, Jordan Dane's premiere novel in her three book series (which sold in auction in 2006) is a romantic suspense. Dane has won numerous writing competitions and her writing skill shows in No One Heard Her Scream. 
 The book is set in San Antonio, Texas. Although Dane no longer lives in San Antonio, she clearly remembers the town well and captures its heart. 
 From the opening prologue to the final chapter, the story moves along, pulling the reader into the mystery. But the strongest aspect of the book is the romantic tension between the two lead characters. If you don't like sex scenes, though, this is not the book for you. 
 If you like modern romantic suspense, with the emphasis on the romance, you'll most likely like No One Heard Her Scream. And since the next two books in Jordan Dane's series are scheduled to come out later this year, you won't have to wait long to read more from her.

text:
"I was going to jail. 
 Worse my arch nemesis would be the one to drag me from my own paranormal museum." 
 Pressed to Death by Kirsten Weiss starts with the above lines; the cozy, possibly paranormal mystery novel is exciting, quick-paced and fun. 
 Maddie, the present owner of San Benedetto's Paranormal Museum, is the unlucky person who discovers the body of a man ahead of wine festival. To make things worse, the same man had accused her of stealing his antique grape press and told the police as much. 
 Maddie is then forced/asked - which ever you decide - to investigate the man's murder, with her former school nemesis Laurel Hammer being right on her tail and constantly trying to drag her to jail, especially after Maddie accidentally set Hammer's hair on fire. 
 While investigating, Maddie can't help but notice that her mother is acting strangely and so is her mother's entire group, the Ladies' Aid. 
 "It was one thing for me to discover a dead body, another to suspect my mom had some knowledge of the crime." 
 After the discovery of the dead body, a Romeo Paganini, Maddie keeps telling herself that she wouldn't interfere with the investigation, especially after the last one nearly got her killed. 
 "This investigation--" 
 "I'm not going to interfere." 
 "Oh yes you are, Madelyn." 
 As with the previous book, Pressed to Death sees Maddie investigating a case that is supposed to be the police's responsibility as well as a historical cold case pertaining to her recently-acquired antique grape press. 
 A relatable character, I absolutely loved Maddie, even more than in the first book in the series. She has a strong sense of what is right and what is wrong, even if that means that her actions will hurt her. She is also caring, has good instincts and has learnt to trust them. This is significant for her character development. 
 Narrated from the first person perspective of Maddie, Pressed to Death allows the reader to see how Maddie's mind works as an amateur sleuth, and engrosses the reader in the novel, the events and the mystery-ies. 
 "Haven't you ever seen something you can't explain?" 
 "Yeah, the way people tend to drop dead in your vicinity, and it's never your fault." 
 There were a lot of beautiful lines and images in the novel. The characters are down-to-earth and I liked the friendship Maddie, Harper and Adele have. 
 "I wanted to evoke the romance and mystery of tea, using lush descriptive phrases." 
 "Lush? These are pornographic," Harper said. "No wonder people were snatching them up." 
 Pressed to Death is the second instalment in The Perfectly Proper Paranormal Museum series, but can be easily read as a standalone novel. 
 Overall, Pressed to Death is a perfect Halloween read and enjoyable cozy mystery. 
 Overall rating: 5 stars 
 Note: I received a free copy of Pressed to Death by Kirsten Weiss in exchange for an honest review as part of a blog tour by Lori Great Escapes Book Tours.

text:
3 Whispering Stars 
 Is it a gift or curse? 
 Eloise had the perfect family until a normal day turned into a nightmare, splitting her family in half. A fatal accident ripped her soul mate and one daughter from her, leaving her and her other daughters life and heart in shattered pieces. It was right then that she noticed a change, a change that either serves her as a curse or gift. 
 Still grieving the loss of her loved ones Eloise is confused, scared and somewhat helpless what's going on why she all of the sudden can hear and see things no one else can. 
 Lisa Unger wrote a quick but intriguing and suspenseful short story, giving the reader a taste of her ability to captivate them with her skillful storytelling. The Whispers scratches the surface of supernatural, thriller and suspense; so if you like such genre I do recommend it, especially since at the end of this novelette you can read an exclusive preview of Lisa Unger's next thriller: CRAZY LOVE YOU (which sounds amazing!!). The Whispers is the first of three mini-series featuring Eloise's life and then in book three that of her granddaughter. 
 Her writing style left me craving for more and I'll definitely check out her full length psychological suspense novel, CRAZY LOVE YOU .

While these are a minor part of the story, they take what could be a caricature character and turn her into a real person who has her own demons and her own code of conduct. 
 The mystery is a good one and it creates tension for the main characters on a very personal level. Everything does not turn out hunky dory for every character, even those we have grown to love. This book was ok. I purchased it on a recommendation but now it's finished I've decided it's not a keeper so off to the rounds of the family it goes (maybe one of them will like it better). 
 It seemed to me that there were some great ideas in this but I just couldn't connect with the characters. Especially Jacob's wife her paranoia seemed very much imposed on her rather than integrated into her personality. Perhaps we should have seen a chapter from her POV just prior to 'the bank statements'. And then it seems all is happy again and she doesn't hold any grudges about what her husband put her through. 
 The idea of being able to communicate with people in a coma via MRI intrigued me (and sent me diving down google rabbit holes) so that was a pro for this book. It did seem strange though that the prior attempt of this with Amy got 'stuck' on the activity of tennis and that when she didn't respond as expected it was abandoned, maybe it was part of the testing protocol but it seemed a bit peculiar. 
 Simon was a definite enigma considering the role it turned out he played and I can see the utility in having him only revealed as he appeared to others. I do wonder though that when the trial comes at the end that there was difficulty in extraditing him due to his crimes in other constituencies. So we're to believe that either through synchronicity he is identified as being the perpetrator for all of these crimes at the same time, or that after Alex identities him as a viable suspect that all of these police forces say "Oooh that's our man" for x. Hmmm 
 I won't be recommending this to anyone but I have started it on the rounds rather than sending it straight to the donation pile so there is that. (Although if I hadn't happened to see my mother 30mins after I finished it the outcome may have been different.

text:
An enjoyable, if not meandering read. 
 Format: Hardcover Vine Customer Review of Free Product 
 I'm reviewing the latest Karin Slaughter book, The Good Daughter. When two girls are forced into the woods at gunpoint, one runs for her life and the other is left behind. 28 years later we visit to discover "Who is the good daughter?". This was my pick for my most highly anticipated July read, so what did I think? 
 ^^ [Blows out a long puff of air] #TheGoodDaughter is another stonker of a book. Weighing in at approx 585 pages, you can imagine how big it is. Now this is not a problem, but it does make me wonder if all of it is going to be necessary, even before I started the book. And I have to say I don't think it all was. 
 ^^ Yes, this is a great story. Between the pages there's love, laughter, loss and sadness. I was truly taken by this family and all they went through, then and now. 
 ^^ Yes, Karin Slaughter can definitely write well, and easily made me feel for her characters; their pain, their heartbreak, the good times and the bad. This psychological thriller is all about the family drama, the terrible things the two girls went through, how their family suffered, and how they finally found themselves and their new roles in life. Albeit with the emotional and physical scars, to remind them of their suffering. 
 ^^ But no, to too much detail. Now, I understand I have an ARC copy and the final edition could be whittled down a lot, and I'm not supposed to moan too much about 'editing' because of this, I cannot help but point out that I felt some of the chapters were just too long and a bit meandering. I also understand this provides great insight to each character, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but I do think it's a point to mention when I found myself skim-reading some of the slower chapters. You know, those meaning to give you a bit of breathing space in between the fast paced action ones. Trouble is, there wasn't enough action packed scenes for me either. 
 ^^ In addition, I think the "Who is the good daughter?" theme is slightly misleading, unless I just didn't get it, I never did find out. Maybe this is why this is the first of a new series, and the best is yet to come? 
 ^^ I take it someone must have told her about the rhyming thing... The Good Daughter by Karin Slaughter? 
 Overall: An enjoyable, if not meandering read. I'm a fan of Karin Slaughter's work, and have to say that although this is not my favourite book of hers, I'm now eager to read the following books in the series to see how this book falls into place with those to come. Although, I'm not sure what is left when this book covers everything... Sadly, three stars, which fits with Amazon's "It's OK", rating. It wasn't awful, it wasn't my next rave about book, just okay. 
 What did you think?

text: A bittersweet read, since I am now officially caught up on Karen Rose- with no new novels available for about six months. Boo. At least if I have to take a hiatus, it's with the memory of one of her better novels to keep me company. Silent Scream's hero is David Hunter, and I've been waiting for his story for quite some time. I like the way Rose kind of switched things up in this book, in that the male lead was the one with the secret traumatic past and a present full of community service, charity and volunteer work done as penance for his mistakes and faults. David was the perfect partner for Olivia, the somewhat stoic detective with a kind and generous heart. The romance and the suspense was spot on and resulted in a great story. I also loved reading the extra epilogue which was available on Rose's website- it gave loyal readers a glimpse at all the happy couples that they've been reading about in the past ten books. Forrest brings the world of Detective Kate Delafield and the series full circle in this latest and what seems to be final installment. I immediately was thrown back into the second book, Murder at the Nightwood Bar, and love how Forrest pushes Delafield to confront her own worst enemy - herself. But the friends she made in that book are here again, especially Maggie, and new friends emerge in unexpected ways. 
 It's been a 30-year journey with Detective Delafield and she ages as we do. Despite the long hiatus since the last book, I was immediately caught up in the journey and the characters. Forrest's characters feel real and she puts them in situations, many that are too true to life, that hit our emotional buttons, bringing us on a ride that excites, scares, and even brings joy.

text: Enthralling stories of the lives of several families are the backdrop for this novel. The hook that catches you is the envelope found by Cecilia in her husband's handwriting that simple reads, "Only to be opened after my death." Now, of course, you know she is going to open it but when and so I could not stop reading until she did---Wow a pretty important secret!. The neighbors in this suburb of Sydney, Australia, seem to be so different but there lives and connected in numerous ways. Failed marriages, adultery, bicycle accidents, and even accidental death or perhaps murder are present in this novel. It is an engaging and exciting read. There are short chapters so you think well just one more chapter and before you know it you are halfway through the book. Well defined and interesting characters are included and the interplay of emotions and actions never subsides. Moreover, at the end the author has an epilogue and "what might have happened" if the husband's actions (which led to his secret) had not occurred. Great read and intellectually stimulating.

text:
This one was fun. In the front of the book is a map of "Soledad County" which sits on the Northern California coast between Humboldt and Mendocino. At the north end of the County there is Oilville, obviously Petrolia, at the south end is Westhaven, the coast road is 1 and over on the inland side winds Highway 101, through the redwoods. A few familiar names like Castle Rock and Eel River, and there you have the setting. 
 Muller does a great job evoking the North Coast folks, including the dope growers, former hippies/commune dwellers, artists, hard drinking rednecks, etc. Oh and of course the Second Home rich folks from the City. There is a mystery with clues strewn around (I admit I was leaning toward the red herrings of the suicidal deputy and the wacko father for a time) and there is a side story of budding romance between the protagonist, a female deputy, and a writer who has come to Soledad to research some murders that took place 13 years earlier. 
 This one was from 2001 and I hope there has been at least one later one with the same characters. A really nice one-night stand, very entertaining. 
 As for what I learned? Large Print is great for reading a whole book in bed.

It isn't as though I didn't know what I was getting into - the title of the book is quite clear - but the body count in this book was pretty high. It's a roller coaster ride and mostly improbable, but I was willing to suspend belief most of the time. 
 The good: The set-up of the conflict and bringing Jack Reacher into the action was well done and suspenseful. The good guys are likable for the most part, and the bad guys are bad, even if we don't get a lot of fleshing out of characters. The action is ongoing and the suspense is pretty good. 
 The bad: Jack Reacher shrugs. A lot. He's also a little self-satisfied and smug in regards to the female love interest (I struggled to buy in to that one) which wraps itself up a little too conveniently. 
 I have heard that the series improves, and I enjoyed this one pretty well, so I'll keep reading them.

text:
In an insular coal mining village in the Midlands, a husband, his wife and their small son have disappeared. The community- already laid low by a wide-spread, mysterious illness- seeks help from Scotland Yard's finest. Inspector Day, Sergeant Hammersmith and Dr. Kingsley are up for the challenge, and are confident they'll be headed back to London on the next morning's train. Unfortunately, this little town holds more than its share of secrets and the investigative trio might find that this case involves more than they can handle. 
 With a wonderfully creepy setting, and plenty of twists, turns and complications, I very much enjoyed this novel. Grecian has a strong sense of time and place, and easily transports readers to a dismal English countryside during the late 1800s. His well-developed main characters Day and Hammersmith are especially charming, and I loved visiting with them and getting to know more about what makes them tick, and how their partnership bonds are strengthening.

text:
Poe Montgomery is wearing his father's patience very thin. He's 23, virtually jobless, and just got picked up by the police, again, for making graffiti art-criminal mischief, in this case. His father, Landon, pours out his woes over Poe's aimless life to his best friend, Jericho McAslan and Jericho feels a kinship to Poe's situation. Jericho had been a handful, and far more trouble to his caregivers at a younger age than Poe is now, but he'd been given the opportunity to learn the trade of tattooing and it saved his life. Now, twenty years later, Jericho's in position to pay it forward, and offers to take Poe on as a receptionist at his tattoo parlor, with the bonus that if he is diligent Jericho will offer him an apprenticeship as a tattoo artist. 
 Poe is a little sulky about the prospect, but he soon is intrigued by the art happening all around him. And, it helps that Jericho is exactly as sexy up-close and personal as Poe had found him when Jericho would pop over for beers with his dad. In fact, Jericho thinks nothing of the age gap between them, and he's not shy of his interest. Jericho's undeniably turned on, but he's also put off by the prospect of damaging his friendship with Landon, and also with the power imbalance in their work relationship. He turns Poe away again and again, but Poe's attitude only gets worse, and he's soon in trouble again with his tagging pals-mot notably Blue. Blue wants all of Poe's attention and he's not afraid to demand it, which makes their friendship uncomfortable for the first time in years. Blue doesn't want Poe to learn how to tattoo, or to find a job where he can be supported by his art-because Blue thinks they ought to suffer for it, and it's all a little off-kilter. Poe hadn't seen how out-there Blue was until he stepped away and got perspective. He wants a good life, with a good man, and Jericho finally comprehends how good he and Poe could be together. And, it's super-duper hot, folks. The best of Daddy porn on the page. 
 I don't want to give away too much more, but I will say that Blue messes things up for Poe and Jericho big time, and it surely ties into the next book in this series. I've read a few tattoo-artist romances this summer and this ones just delightful. The age difference was fun to observe, and the relationships between Poe and his dad, Landon, and Landon and Jericho are really awesome. Landon became a father at a young age and raised Poe without help for nearly all his life. The lack of maternal coddling in their youth is a bonding point for Jericho and Poe, and the way Landon manages to not punch Jericho in the face for "exploiting" his boy is charming. I liked all these characters and felt like they were real enough I'd go have a beer with them anytime. I look forward to the next book where I expect Blue will get a strong lesson in adulting, and love. 
 I received a review copy via NetGalley.

text:
This contemporary M/M romance is a slow building, delightful love story. 
 Greg is a single father with full custody of his ten-year old son, Davey. He is an architect, with a thriving business, and had been scouted for the Major leagues in baseball as a young man. He is also gay. When the story opens, Greg is at Davey's little league game, but Davey struggles at-bat. Another spectator, who happens to be an ophthalmologist, suggests getting Davey's vision checked. The prognosis, after many tests, is bleak: Davey is going blind. This shatters Greg, and Davey. 
 At a picnic, Tom meets Greg and is attracted, not only by Greg's appearance, but with the compassion and love Greg shows to his son. See, Tom was raised with everything a life of privilege offered, except parental affection. He was largely cared for by nannies, and he longs to find a loving relationship that would include children. To date, all the men Tom has dated were attracted to his money. He reaches out to Greg and they decide to try dating. 
 Witnessing the anguish Greg has for Davey's lost vision, and the loss of his fun-loving games, Tom does some research. It turns out there's some new team-style games that visually impaired kids/adults are playing. One of these is 'beep baseball' and Tom dives in to assemble local support for a league. Greg is blown away by Tom's effort to help Davey acclimate to his new blindness. In fact, he's a bit suspicious of Tom's motives. 
 All questionable motives aside, Tom really just wants to spend more time with Greg. Their fledgling relationship is tried and tested when Greg's ex-wife arrives, following years of neglect, to 'save Davey's vision' with a miracle gene therapy cure. Greg is hesitant to discount any chance of reversing Davey's blindness, but the risks clearly outweigh the potential for healing. And, Tom is there to help Greg make the hard decision. 
 Plus, Tom is great at making Davey feel like a normal kid. He's the kind of guy Davey would like to see his dad settle down with, in fact. 
 It's a slow build into the physical. Tom wants to take things slow to make sure he has real feelings for Greg, and Greg is overwhelmed with the responsibility of caring for a newly-blind child. I really appreciated the author's sensitivity in holding off, and in having Tom fully commit to a real relationship rather than jumping into bed. 
 Both characters were very well-developed and the arc of Davey's transition from poorly sighted to completely blind--and as a functional blind person--was heart-remanding and terrifyingly interesting. I loved he community that Greg and Tom shared--gay, but also some had visual or speech deficits. I haven't read the two previous books in this series, but I strongly suspect that other couples' romances had been featured. This is a gentle romance with steady growth of both protagonists into a relationship that seems likely to flourish. I really enjoyed it!

See full review for Every Boy's Got One at: https://toomanybooksnotenoughshelves.... 
 Jane Harris is excited, for the first time in her life she is leaving the wonderful NYC so she can go to Italy. Because her best friend is eloping and she can't do so without her best friend/maid of honor. Of course, she might be a little bit too excited as she buys a few bottles of water for the trip and the guy behind her snorts. Not to mention the guy behind her starts a really loud phone conversation about something or other that she has to wonder what stick is up his ass? But she doesn't have time to wonder, because Holly and Mark were supposed to meet her at the gate with Mark's best friend Cal and she hasn't seen them anywhere, what if they died in a horrible traffic accident? 
 They eventually do show up and it turns out that the guy who was behind Jane earlier is Mark's best friend Cal. She is slightly disappointed to learn this information, but she won't let it get her down about finally leaving the country or the fact that her best friend is getting married. She'll get to know Cal and everything will be fine! Except it won't when Cal turns out to be a foreign correspondent for the NY Journal, who's finally come home only to be whisked away for his best friend's elopement, because he doesn't believe in marriage. And he plans to try and convince Mark that this whole elopement thing is a bad idea. 
 So I have to admit that this book in the Boy series wasn't my favorite when I read it over four years ago. Compared to the other two books, it was kind of dry and I didn't really like the fact that both parties - Cal and Jane - had a mutual dislike for each other from the get go. Now, four years later, it was actually entertaining to read.

text:
Corin and Skylar are people from very different worlds who meet via their roommates in college. 
 Corin is a hardened gal who's been used and abused by those she's loved and took off for LA to get the education she always dreamed of. She meets Layla at school, and feels rather protective of this innocent young freshman. She's especially not happy with Layla's ex, Landen, who seems to be emotionally unstable. 
 Skylar's pretty sure his roommate and soccer teammate, Landen, is certifiable. The way he's completely gone over Layla is shocking, to say the least. Now, her redheaded, snarky roommate Corin? That girl is a total dynamo. For Skylar, a wealthy son who couldn't buy his parents' attention, Corin's a challenge he'd love to meet. 
 As Layla and Landen's romance goes boom, bust, and boom again, Corin and Skylar join forces to keep everyone stable--as best they can--and develop a strong friendship. Which Skylar wants to turn into more, and Corin's afraid will totally destroy what little self-esteem she's cobbled together. 
 The book spans several years, and I think that was a bit too ambitious, because I would have liked to be more 'in the moment' with these two. Rather, it felt kinda rushed and didn't really experience much in the romance aspect. There was clearly enough story to build into two books. There's a lot of filthy talk, and that seemed a little out-of-place for 19 year old kids, to be honest. My biggest gripe was with the editing, however, and I can only hope that the many errors I encountered in the book were corrected in the edition that went to print. I received an ARC on release day, though, so I'm nervous that I got the finalized book, and that would be a shame if it's true. 
 The true romance really picks up about 60% into the book, but it's still more drama than romance. Teeny bit of sexytimes, for the length of the book. I did like the story, and I'm glad I got to see these characters again.

4.5 awesome stars 
 I was so excited to read this, like ridiculously excited. As in, I stopped everything to read this. I had very high expectations, and thankfully, was not let down. 
 I was a little confused at first, as I've seen this title referred to as part of the Castles Ever After series on one website and The Spindle Cove series on another. Well, which one is it? It's BOTH! Yaass! 
 Imagine that the game of clue and James Bond somehow had a secret love child. That is this book. Except I would take Piers over Bond any day. I mean, come on. 
 Piers and Charlotte are caught together hiding behind the curtains in a library and are wrongly assumed to be lovers meeting for a tryst. In fact, Charlotte had sought Piers out to warn him of her marriage minded mother and her inevitable plans to force the two of them together. While talking, they hear people approaching and hide. Enter a couple that decides they do want to have a tryst. Loudly. Enthusiastically. When all is said and done, it is Charlotte and Piers that are caught together alone, not the lovers. Enter the common forced-by-perceived-impropriety-marriage-of-convenience plot. Piers is surprised to find himself more than willing, while Charlotte would rather...not. Charlotte decides that if she can solve the mystery of the unidentified lovers, she can clear her name of scandal and prevent herself from being forced into marriage with someone who has made it clear he wants no part of love. 
 It's a simple plot, but she does it so well. What makes Tessa Dare's books so great is that they are so damned funny. I have yet to get through one without laughing out loud more than once. Her books are escapism at it's finest. That's not to say the book was perfect. There were a few times I rolled my eyes. Misunderstandings that would have been easily solved by just, you know, talking, are a common problem in a lot of romance novels. There's a fine line between creating necessary angst and characters being just plain obtuse. Then again, sometimes people really are just obtuse. 
 Regardless, I hope these books continue on forever. Invent new characters, I don't care. Tell me they were there from the start, and I'll just go along with it. They are just such a pleasure to read.

This is an odd-couple story of two neighbors. There is NO steam, here. 
 Anders is an introvert who lives by a rigid schedule and prefers to keep his neighbors outside of his door. He's startled out of his carapace by Finch who is a social butterfly and insists on having his way with Anders--and I mean this in a romantic sense, though there is nothing beyond a kiss in this book. 
 Finch is that kid in school who continually poked you in the back, or whispered to you just when the teacher was sure to turn in your direction. He's impulsive and irritating, and Anders is overwhelmed by his friendliness assault. No one wants to be Anders' friend, and he's pretty okay with that. 
 I did find Finch to be endearing as the story went on, and the way that he opened Anders' shell, mostly to inject a bit of sand in there, was quirky-funny. He did take Anders and leave him alone, in a way. He didn't insist Anders become jovial or even nice. He simply shoved all his friendliness at him and hoped a bit of it stuck. And, it did, sorta. I really liked how Anders stopped existing in his life and began making choices to live in it--by meeting people and connecting with them. His big realization scene had a rom-com feel, complete with police intervention and Pretty Woman rescue, which was endearing. 
 I, myself, prefer a romance to have a bit of steam, and the lack of it is generally disappointing. I can't say I'm THAT disappointed by the lack here, mostly because I didn't get the same thrill of these two guys connecting as I generally do. I think that I didn't connect with the characters that well and, as such, I wasn't put-off that I had no sexytimes of theirs to experience. *shrugs* 
 For people who like odd-couples, brash characters, and low-steam romances this will likely hit them in the sweet spot.

text:
Pride and Prejudice is a story of how two different worlds collide. Wherein a proud -and very wealthy-man, Mr. Darcy's, and the prejudiced full-of-wit Ms. Bennet's paths crossed and they then realize that sometimes the last person on earth you want to be with is the one person you can't be without. 
 The characters are very much believable, albeit some are too obnoxiously haughty (*cough* Mr. Collins and Ms. Caroline Bingley *cough*) they make me want to tug the hair out of my scalp. No one is too kind to the point of surrealism - Bingley almost reached that level, thank the heavens, he 'abandoned' Jane (courtesy of his sister and Mr. Darcy), which puts him to a different level. They're all like real walking people, who think like average people (with the exception of Mrs. Bennet). At first, the author made us think that Bingley is perfect, but as his character unravel we've realized that he isn't. Charlotte also seemed like an ideal bestfriend, but she has her fair share of flaws too. By marrying Collins, it showed that safety of income is what matters to her the most, not love nor happiness. 
 Mr. Darcy, who at first, according to Lizzy, "a very disagreeable man" will grow into you page by page. It was like the characters unfold and reveal their true nature slowly and before you know it, they're already the opposite of what you've once perceived them as. Just like, Mr. Darcy, at first I, myself, agrees to Lizzy that he is really proud and just a pain in the arse. I mean, come on, he referred to Lizzy as "not handsome enough" and he seems so snobbish and arrogant. But it turns out that he's just shy! This shows that you shouldn't judge someone so carelessly and easily. Get to know them first and then feel free to state your opinion afterwards. 
 I think their story is the root of all the "enemies-at-first-then-lovers-in-second" romances. Basically, Lizzy and Darcy did nothing but dance around in circles. Their story went on like this: Lizzy and Darcy met on a ball (designed for Mr.Bingley's arrival). Darcy ignored everyone and insulted Lizzy. They started bantering like children. And then as Bingley and Jane are getting to know each other, they started seeing each other too and feel something...that they shouldn't feel towards the other. Darcy took interest in Lizzy because she's so different. (now, I'm pretty sure the P&P is really where all the authors of the new era, get the inspirations from their characters. Because that's how the main guy in books always notices and started liking the girl, by her ignoring him.) Anyway, Mr. Darcy builds up his walls to try and keep Lizzy on arm's length but he failed. The lady's getting under his skin. And when he couldn't stand it no more, he just accepted the fact that he's in love with her. So, he proposed and she declined because of what he'd done to Jane and Bingley's relationship. Darcy's ego fell 300 feet below the ground and so they're back to square one. 
 I liked two characters on this book - Lizzy's parents. They're polar opposites that it makes me wonder how they ended up with each other. But the one I enjoyed the most is, probably, Lizzy's mom, Mrs.Bennet. I have a soft spot for mothers and she's the only one - I'm pretty sure - who made me laugh. 
 Unlike most of the people who've read the book, I didn't like Mr. Darcy that much. Though at some part he made me smile. I think Lizzy's alright and is really smart. There's this line of her that made me like her so much: 
 "I only want to think you perfect, and you set yourself against it. Do not be afraid of my running into any excess, of my encroaching on your privilege of universal good-will. You need not. There are few people whom I really love, and still fewer of whom I think well. The more I see of the world, the more am I dissatisfied with it; and every day confirms my belief of the inconsistency of all human characters, and of the little dependence that can be placed on the appearance of merit or sense." 
 And also in some strange universe, I liked Lydia's character. She remained herself till the end. 
 I chose this book because it's been something that I really want to come to, for long. I've tried to read this book so many times before but I always tend to lose interest before I even reach halfway. So now it became a challenge for me to really finish P&P this time - I so want to know what's all the fuss about Mr. Darcy and Lizzy's story. I have really high expectations regarding this book and such a shame that it did not meet the said expectations. 
 Now let's start with the famous first line of the book - which I find very, very disagreeable. 
 "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife." 
 I don't think so. Not all men desires a wife (especially, those "single" men who have "possession of a good fortune"). Not even in their era. Some men just want to live alone, to work for their selves, or to gamble their money without worrying about their family. Some wants to have flings with women and live freely without any ties - living the bachelor life. So that line is a big no-no for me. 
 Believe me when I say that I tried so hard to like this book. I really hate it when I'm one of that 1% who didn't enjoy the most-treasured books of everyone. The story line's not that good; it's a bit shallow if you'll ask me. The characters are alright. The ending doesn't have that much impact. Usually the endings are the most emotional part (for the readers) of the book, because it is the end. But I didn't get so attached to it that I finished the book feeling...nothing. The writing style is good but...complicated - really complicated. It is the main reason why I did not enjoy this book that much. For instance there's this line: 
 "Shall we ask him why a man of sense and education, and who has lived in the world, is ill qualified to recommend himself to strangers?" 
 I was pondering on what does the italicized line could meant, turns out that it means, "shy". Shy! Why did Jane Austen have to make lines like that?! Is this some sort of torture? Maybe it's the trend on their era? But I don't know about them, I don't see the logic in using super-profound-poetic-lines on stating such simple ideas. There are also times where I have to re-read a paragraph because I failed to understand it the first time. 
 I also noticed that there are some misspelled words (such as sopha, teaze, chuse, exstacy, etc.). I'm not even sure if that's how they spell the said words back then. 
 They say that at first you won't enjoy this book, but the second time around you'll realize how good it is. Too bad, I'm not planning to read it again. 
 What was your favorite part of the book? 
 When Mrs. Bennet didn't allowed Jane to borrow the carriage to go to the Bingley's. I had a good laugh at her selfish plan for Jane and Bingley. 
 Do you have a least favorite part of the book? 
 When Darcy paid Mr. Wickham just to marry Lizzy's little sister, Lydia. I was shaking my head the whole time at how naive Lydia is, but I can't blame her for she is only "inlove". . And I dislike Mr. Wickham, with a passion. He's a cunning, deceptive arse. 
 --- 
 I won't recommend this to anyone I know. (Unless you have a Webster-type vocabulary) It's a struggle to read or is it just me? And there are lots of dull moments, that make me drift off. I also feel like this book can be compressed in 10 pages if all the irrelevant scenes were to be removed. 
 If you're a fan of classic-lit you'll like this one. Also those who love romances and snobbish main hero would enjoy this. This book is definitely for people who have a lot of patience and time - which is definitely not me.

Each character has their own complex motivations for their behavior, and Karina refreshingly lets the reader form their own opinions about the characters. I don't want to describe the plot in detail here because Shooting Scars is a very intricate tale that is best enjoyed fresh. 
 Shooting Scars is filled with lots of action, romance and twists and turns. Is it painful? Hell, yes. And that is why it is such an amazing story. My problem? I need Bold Tricks like, yesterday.

4 Harmonizing stars 
 Source: eARC for Honest Review Courtesy of Author and Enticing Journey Book Promotions 
 Genre: MM Adult Contemporary Romance 
 Standalone 
 My Imperfect Harmony Review . . . 
 This is my second Jay Northcote book and I may be a bit smitten with her and her books. Imperfect Harmony first has a great cover to pull you in then it ends up being a sweet book about second chances to complete the whole package. 
 John Fletcher is heart broken after the tragic loss of his partner, whom he was with for 22 years. He's now just plotting through life but not experiencing it. He's given up his passion for music and is now just existing. Rhys Callington, is a young man who is also heart broken after the loss of his partner but thankfully he still has music to keep him going but not thriving. 
 There were enough parallels with his own experience. 
 John's neighbor needs his help getting around after her hip replacement. One of the errands is taking her go to choir. At first he's resistant to coming to participate but once his heart starts to beat a little faster after seeing the choir director, a young handsome spunky man, he takes a chance and joins in. 
 As soon as John started to sing again he knew what he's been missing and now has a new want in life where a hole now exists. At first these two start just as friends, especially with a large age gap between the two but the more they get to know each the more they wanted from each other. 
 Since, both of their experiences mirror each other, their union is a very cathartic journey for each of them by finally moving forward together after their losses. 
 ~You have to go on without me. ~ 
 Even though they have many similarities with their stories and their passion for music, but they also had many differences especially with where they are both at in life. For Rhys, the age difference means nothing to John. But for John he has a few fears and issues causing him to not be as open to all possibilities as Rhys is. 
 " . . . You only get to live it once, and only you can decide what's right, But if you want my advice, it's this: say yes. Say yes to the chance of love and happiness. Don't let it slip away from you. . . . " 
 With everything on the line for a chance of happiness there's a lot to lose if they both can't get on the same page. 
 "Chin up, love. Now come on. Let's get singing. You're always telling us how therapeutic it is. None of your troubles will seem so bad after a good sing." 
 I absolutely adored Rhys and John together. I'm smitten with this story. I appreciated so much that it wasn't filled with tons of angst. Instead it was a heartfelt story where you got to feel both of their pains but also got to experience their raw healing while they blended their harmonies together. The story felt real yet charming and the little nuances that John and Rhys had just made them more loveable. If you are a fan of Cardeno C. then Jay Northcote is another great MM author to turn to for sweet loving heartfelt stories.

-_- You have got to be kidding me!! That's it?? That's the epic love story of Rush and Blair? In less than 65 000 words? I don't believe this, there must be a mistake. 
 Don't get me wrong, I really liked Never Too Far, the sex scenes were hot (Where was Rush's barbell?!?!?!?!) and the fluffy scenes between Rush and Blair were cute and sweet. But something was missing and I'm not just talking about Rush's barbell. I just can't say what it is but something definitely has changed. 
 Like the characters. The characters changed a lot. 
 Blaire became infinitely more likeable, she's still the insecure, neurotic Mary-Sue she was in the first book. But now...her determination to provide for her baby's needs first. Her independence. It's all quite admirable, really. 
 But unlike Blaire, Rush's character had gotten even worse!!! I know right, how is that even possible??/ 
 He spends most of the novel either sucking up to Blaire- 
 "She's amazing. No... she's perfect. Everything about her is fucking perfect," I said aloud. "I don't just love her, she owns me. Completely. I'd do anything for her." 
 -or begging for forgiveness. 
 "I'll be whatever you allow me to be, Blaire. Just don't shut me out again. Please." 
 The rest of the times, he seems to threatening other people who might be potential suitors for Blaire. 
 "You stay away from her. Do you hear me? Back the fuck off. Blaire loves me; she's just confused and hurt. She's also very vulnerable. So help me God, if you even think you're going to take advantage of her current state I will beat the shit out of you." 
 Rush's emotions are all over the place and it's all because of this one exception, Blaire Wynn. 
 "No man has ever loved a woman as much as I love you. Nothing will ever come before you. I don't know what else I have to do to prove to you that I won't let you down again. I won't hurt you. You don't have to be alone anymore. I need you." 
 Rush is deeply in love with Blaire and I know love can change a person, but it can't change a person that much! What happened to the sexy, bad boy we met in Fallen Too Far? Where did his saucy retorts disappear to? Instead Rush develops into this overly sentimental, increasingly possessive and aggressive guy. 
 I don't quite envy Blaire at this point. But Rush is still who he is, and because of the loyalty I feel to him, I feel obligated to say the positive side of things. His protectiveness can be adorably cute and sexy at the same. And his urge to defend Blaire made me hoot for him. But I mostly wanted to tell him to calm the hell down.

PURE PERFECTION!! 
 I could read only Kristen Ashley books and be very happy. RIDE STEADY is another slam-dunk winner from the Queen of Alphas, with a story that ripped my heart out and characters that I won't soon forget. Joker might be one Ms. Ashley's most unforgettable Alphas ever, a man who rose from a painful and loveless childhood to become a patched-in Brother of the Chaos MC. Chaos became his family, and the MC recognized the fire burning in Joker that would serve the club well. 
 "He was at the shop window, empty pockets, face pressed to the glass, starin' at what he wanted but couldn't have. I'll wager, to survive, he's banked that fire. We gotta help him direct it and make sure if it flares bright, it doesn't burn him out." 
 Carissa Teodoro's life becomes entwined with Joker's, as the two former high school classmates meet again years later. Let me just say that this book is so incredibly gripping and heartbreaking and sexy, that I am tempted to re-read it to experience these feelings all over again! She was once the golden girl who had it all, and he was the boy from the wrong side of the tracks. Their story spans years and that is what I love about Ms. Ashley's writing: there is no Insta-love here, instead, our hero and heroine have a shared history that adds a depth and richness to this book. 
 "Yeah, Carrie," he answered. "It's you. It's always been you. It'll always be you. Fuckin' always." 
 Joker is a sexy, bad-ass Alpha biker that has zero interest in relationships, or in real friendships for that matter, since he has a hard time opening up to anyone about his feelings or his past. That is what makes his relationship with Carrie so poignant: this is a man who is so closed off and afraid of emotional bonds that he has been alone (and lonely) most of his life. 
 Carrie draws his out just by being herself. She is going through a messy and painful divorce, has a baby, is struggling to make ends meet and has a ton of emotional baggage. She is not perfect but she is open to love and gives her heart unconditionally to Joker. 
 "Rule," he stated instantaneously. 
 His strange word made me blink at the lockers. "Sorry?" 
 "Rule. You can't be like that on the phone. You can only be like that when I can kiss you." 
 I lifted a hand and pressed it to the cold steel of my locker, leaning into it because my knees suddenly wouldn't support me. 
 "You hear me?" he asked. "Yes, Joker." 
 OH. EM. GEE!! *SWOON* I can't say enough about Ride Steady. Plus some of my favorite bad-ass Alphas from Ms. Ashley's other books make appearances here! Dead. There is also a sneak peek at the next Chaos book at the end of Ride Steady and it sounds amazing. Joker and Carissa's story is beautiful, thrilling and passionate. Ride Steady is a must-read! 
 Favorite quotes: 
 "Butterfly, you're cute all the time, cuter some times more than others, and it's fucked up because right now you're bein' a pain in the ass and this is one of those times that you're cuter. But you gotta get this so you can get over it. My old man doesn't exist for me. I left him and that life behind, and I don't want it back in any way it can come back." 
 "We are who cares about us."

 Source: eARC for Honest Review Courtesy of Simon Pulse via Edelweiss 
 It has been quite awhile since I last visited Sea Breeze and read anything by Abbi Glines. And I'm super happy I did. We all know that Dewayne has a story behind his bad boy player ways and his loyal heart to his friends and family. 
 " . . . It's part of your shield. Underneath, I don't know many men that compare. You're one of the best, Dewayne. One of the best." 
 Dewayne Falco is the last one standing in his group of friends as a single man. Part of him wants what they want but the other part can't fathom giving up his freedom for one magic pussy. 
 Throughout the series Dewayne has always been the misunderstood stand up guy. Here we get to see that he has love donce and had to step aside when his brother liked the same girl. Being the family guy he is, he steps aside but has always loved from a far. When tragedy strikes he wants to help Sienna but she disappears out of nowhere. Which causes Dewayne to go on a six year sex bender trying to get Sienna out of his head. 
 Six years later Dewayne is still loyal but is unaware of his strengths and self worth. When Sienna comes back to Sea Breeze he wants to stay away for her sake thinking she deserves better. Especially after all she has lost and had to sacrifice. 
 "He's a good man. He just doesn't realize it. He doubts himself, but my boy is as good as they come. Always has had a heart of gold. Just need him to wake up 
 and see that." 
 Sienna has always had a soft spot for her best friend's older brother Dewayne but it was just easier and convenient to be with Dustin. Now that Dustin is gone and she was forced away, she's a bit jaded at life. Especially the Falco's but not is all that it seems. What we do know is her parents suck!! The decisions they made were appalling and caused her so much heartache and unnecessary grief. 
 Sienna had high points and low points for me. I get why she was they way she was but her interpretation of things drove me a bit batty, especially because Dewayne is so awesome. 
 I didn't have a lot to offer someone. I got that. But hearing Dewayne say I wasn't enough hit me hard. Really hard. (Ugh! Sienna annoyed more than not because she misinterpreted what Dewayne said all the time. He never said she wasn't enough. Never. But Sienna only hears what she wants to hear.) 
 Dewayne tries to do the right thing but doesn't realize that being with Sienna is the right thing. Once he stops fighting it and gives in to the magic pussy he finally gets 'it'. He gets why all his friends changed. Why they all chose love. Now that he's all in he turns into the sweetest thing. (Well just sweeter than he already was) 
 Once Sienna sees clearly and stops taking things so personally she too gets to find some happiness and see what all that sexual fuss is all about. 
 Highlights of this story for me were: Micah & Dewayne. The low point for me were: Sienna's misinterpretations & Dewayne's lack of self worth. Did I like the story? Yes. Do I like the series? Yes, even though at times its a bit redundant. Will I read the next book in the series? Hell Yes, as we finally get Rock and Trisha's story.

I am calling 'Twist' a friends-to-lovers story because Alex meets her ideal man online and they really do become "friends" even though it is through a dating site. She decides to surprise him and travels all the way to Coeur d'Alene, Idaho. SURPRISE! It turns out she was not communicating with "Eric" but instead was really emailing with Joe, his brother.  "With all the body-shaping underwear, lip gloss, heels, and tiny dress, you could almost say I'd been fibbing about who I was. His lie, however , left my Spanx and push-up bra way behind."

text:
"Oh lord, the things I've yet to do to you. I should warn you...if you ever wander into my private office again, you'll be well and truly ravished right there upon my desk." 
 "Is that a threat or a promise?" 
 "Choose whichever inspires you to misbehave." 
 I don't know if the reason I loved this book so much is that I just finished one of the most depressing, least romantic books I've ever read, or if this book was just wonderful. I have a feeling it's a little of both. Then again, maybe it's the cover. I mean, just look at it. 
 It's a thing of vintage romance cover beauty. 
 The plot is pretty simple. The duke doesn't want to marry/settle down. It isn't that he'd rather sleep with whoever he wants but because he has no desire to be bound to a woman he knows he wouldn't love and watch as her spirit is slowly crushed by his indifference. Gabriel grew up watching his mother waste away because she was married to a man that refused her any kind of affection or even kindness. He saw what his father's indifference and disregard did to his mother and decides he wants nothing to do with marriage. It sounds like a piss poor excuse, but it was explained well. Gabriel decides that his younger brother needs to marry and he'll pass the reins to him. So we have the week-long bride hunting party aka The Bachelor before cameras. Gabriel and his sister know that Tristian is shallow and useless so they appoint themselves as co-bride hunters. They watch the way the chosen seven woman carry themselves, interact with each other, etc... Thrown in the bunch is Madelyn Haywood. She doesn't really fit in but the duke's sister adores her and wants her to have a chance. She's a walking disaster who is mocked endlessly for her accident-prone antics and general bad luck when it comes to not making a fool of herself in one way or another. This is a classic tale of odd free-spirited woman attracting the unattainable brooding duke. 
 While this book is a walking bundle of tropes, it also happens to be everything I love about romance. The beginning of the book stumbled a little because it was just one cliche after another. But as the saying goes, there is a reason something is a cliche. Sure, Gabriel is closed off, brooding, and never smiles. Yes, Madelyn can't walk around a garden without tripping or getting a wasp sting on her ass. Of course, the duke would find her refreshing and different from all of the other women. It's been done a thousand times before but this time, it was just done so well. 
 The writing was great. The kind you don't even notice because it just flows. 
 Honestly, I'd say Gabriel is in my top 10 favorite brooding-alpha-dukes. He's too perfect but that's exactly what I want in my romance novels. That's the whole damn point. He's cold and distant but never unkind. He's stiff and proper but willing to throw propriety out the window for the heroine. Handsome but not conceited. Serious with a wicked sense of humor. Protective with the perfect amount of possessive. Seriously, I could go on and on. And ladies hold on to your pants, the sex was fantastic. AND he's an amazing lover. And generous, as he should be. 
 He thought of her pleasure first and foremost. Without it, his meant nothing, was nothing. 
 Long story short, Gabriel was everything a romance H should be. 
 Madelyn wasn't anything particularly special. But that was part of the charm. Imperfect heroine snags ridiculously perfect H. Some people will probably think it a little over dramatic and flowery. Maybe it was. But it rang true for me. I've always thought a great love story (whether IRL or fiction) should be about two people who each think they got the better deal. This book has that. 
 Yes, there is a misunderstanding. Yes, I find them ridiculously annoying too and just want to scream Just fucking talk to each other. Open your mouth and make words come out. But you know, that's how these things go. 
 Maybe it was just my mood or it just scratched my itch for an actually romantic romance, but I loved it. I went into it expecting a solid 3 star read and came away pleasantly surprised. Not great literature or anything but it's certainly going on my re-read shelf.

text:
I'm a little bummed out once again that I can't give half stars. Actually, if I can rate the first and second halves of the books I would, and I would give the first half 3 stars, and the second half 5 stars. 
 Perhaps I need to read Jane Austen books back to back, so I don't lose the "groove" that it takes me a while to get into when reading them. I have to make my brain work a little harder at the elegant writing style (since there is nothing modern that even compares), and it takes a few chapters to get used to it. Then I have to make sure that I have all my characters and their backstories straight. By the time the last half of the novel comes around, I am really into it. Then I look back after it's finished and think, "wow that was a great book!", even though early on I'm thinking "oh boy, am I ever going to make it through this?" 
 So the story itself was good, but not as good as either Pride and Prejudice or Sense and Sensibility. By the end I was totally connected to Anne and her emotions, and could despise the snobbery surrounding her just as if it was surrounding me. The effects of persuasion in the book are obviously the reason for the title, and that theme was heavy throughout, which I loved. Anne's character drove me crazy for the first half of the book, because I saw her as a weak and easily manipulated person. Very uninteresting to me to watch someone else sit back and live life so passively. Then, like a flip of a switch, I noticed her character take on more self-confidence. I found the other characters more interesting and lively than she was, and felt as if she was a mere observer of life around her. I could understand and pity her and Wentworth because who hasn't been a situation where they wonder what if? But her character was so timid and in the shadows compared to others, I wondered if I wasn't just reading a sad story about a girl who lost her love and then watched him from afar, eight years later, court other women all while she pines in silence. Wasn't working for me. 
 But then something shifted, and I can't tell if it was a shift in the actually story and it was when the author decided to really kick things up, or if it was my issues with getting "into" and Austen novel. Either way, I enjoyed the last half of the book immensely. I couldn't put it down without wanting to immediately pick it back up. 
 The scenes in Lyme were interesting and action packed, and the scenes in bath were wonderful because you got to see a lot of character emerge not only from Anne herself, but from her father, sister, Lady Russell and Mr. Elliot. 
 However, the story didn't match up to P&P or S&S. Pride and Prejudice is my favorite. I think because from the start of that book you have more tension between the lovers-to-be. There is a lot of backstory between Anne and Wentworth, but their interaction is very limited so it doesn't have the tension that P&P has from the start. It isn't until the last quarter of the book that Anne and Frederick really get into good dialogue.

The story of Lilith and her rise to become the powerful and influential head of a high-class call-girl operation is tragic at times and always gripping. Her mother trains her in the ways of the lifestyle, and Vivian will certainly not win any Mother of the Year awards. But she is sure of a woman's power and never lets her daughter forget it. 
 This story spans several decades and is filled with some of the most intense sexual scenes I have ever read. Menage, light BDSM, young girls experiencing their first sexual awakenings, this book has it all. All of the characters spanning the years are fascinating, and the Miami drug scene in the eighties and nineties provides a dangerous backdrop to the main story. 
 M. Robinson has an interesting way of writing where she takes you literally through the life and the mind of the main characters. It is a layered and very rich story, and not exactly for the faint of heart. Ms. Robinson is extremely talented and certainly can bring on the angst! Just please note that this book contains some very graphic erotic scenes and if that is your cup of tea, then you will love The Madam.
